summary:
Allwork.Space reports on CBRE's third-quarter 2026 earnings call, where executives said higher interest rates and broader market uncertainty are causing commercial real estate deals to be repriced, delayed, or restructured as refinancing agreements. The reporting cites CoStar's coverage of the call. CBRE Chair and CEO Bob Sulentic said interest rate volatility is weighing on investment sales, mortgage lending, and development activity, and warned the slowdown could extend into 2027.

Despite that backdrop, CBRE posted strong headline numbers. Global property sales revenue rose 28% year over year in the quarter, with a 37% increase in the United States, led by industrial and retail transactions. Industrial leasing revenue grew 16%. Total revenue increased 13% to $11.5 billion, and net income attributable to the company rose 22% to $443 million. The piece notes a divergence between those results and conditions late in the quarter: capital markets activity slowed in September as some transactions stalled or collapsed entirely.

The article also highlights a structural shift in where corporate real estate money is going. Spending on traditional real estate is weakening in part because large technology companies are redirecting capital toward data centers and critical infrastructure. CBRE's data center infrastructure revenue surged 80% in the third quarter. The company expects critical infrastructure services to produce nearly $4.5 billion of revenue in 2027, with the broader infrastructure services business approaching $7 billion.

The item is a short market and earnings roundup rather than a workplace operations piece. It touches on commercial real estate financing conditions, brokerage performance, and the data center build-out, but contains no material on workplace technology, visitor management, desk or room booking, hybrid and return-to-office policy, workplace analytics, or facilities operations. Note that the supplied text also contains repeated Cloudflare bot-verification boilerplate, which is artifact content rather than editorial material.
